topic: fx: A Tiny, Open, Native Coding Agent
summary: fx is Vercel Labs' experimental coding-agent harness and CLI written in Zig, open sourced under Apache-2.0 on 2026-08-11/17-18 (Vercel Labs product, origin of the `fx.sh` domain). It is a single native binary (~6.2-7.8 MiB depending on target) with no Node.js or Python runtime, a CI-enforced 2 ms startup budget on six command paths, and a ~25.5 KB / ~6,400-7,300-token request floor that is roughly a quarter of Claude Code's harness overhead (29,061 tokens measured). Its real differentiator is not the size brag but four ways to drive one core: an interactive shell that behaves closer to a Unix shell than an IDE-in-the-terminal, one-shot `fx ask --json` for scripts/CI, `fx acp` as an Agent Client Protocol server for editors, and an embeddable WebAssembly/Node SDK published as `libfx` (createFxAgent / createFxTerminal) that runs the agent in a browser. As of 2026-10-01 the repo sits at 3,237 stars / 364 forks / 250 open issues with 84 npm versions and the latest GitHub release v0.0.12 (2026-09-30), and it is still explicitly labeled experimental with breaking changes between releases. Default billing routes through Vercel AI Gateway (default model moonshotai/kimi-k3); Codex (ChatGPT subscription) and Grok (X Premium subscription) OAuth logins and OpenAI-compatible custom connections (Ollama, vLLM, OpenRouter) bypass it. Reviewers converge on the same verdict: excellent as an embeddable harness, not yet a daily-driver replacement for a mature coding assistant.

key_points: Measured (not vibed) review on macOS arm64 with fx v0.0.7 vs Claude Code v2.1.251: `fx --help` 2.7 ms vs `claude --help` 112 ms; launch-to-first-model-request 31 ms; binary 6.19 MiB vs Claude Code's 197 MB.

Deconstructs the '10 microsecond cold start' claim: it measures the time before fx accepts input, not before anything useful happens; the project's own AGENTS.md/CI budget is 2 ms per command on Linux, so the headline is a marketing framing of an engineering budget.

Measured request overhead by pointing undocumented FX_GATEWAY_BASE_URL / FX_GATEWAY_CHAT_URL at a local mock: 25,479 bytes total for a two-word prompt = 17 tool definitions (17,376 B, 68.2%) + base system prompt (5,531 B, 21.7%) + runtime context (2,456 B) + prompt (59 B); ~6,400-7,300 tokens vs Claude Code's 29,061 counted tokens (~4x gap).
MCP tools are not inlined: fx ships `capability_search` + `mcp_select_tool` so a server's schemas only load when selected (lazy tool loading, like Claude Code's tool search).

Hidden cost found: in a normal HOME the same request balloons from 25,479 to 42,727 bytes because fx scans 12 skill directories including `~/.claude/skills`, `~/.codex/skills`, `~/.config/opencode/skills`, `~/.agents/skills`, `~/.claw/skills` and ships a skill catalog (name/description/path) every turn; catalog capped by `skill_catalog_bytes` (default 16 KiB), disable with `off`.

Docs vs binary mismatch at v0.0.7: the docs list ~26 tools but the captured payload contained 17 (e.g. `terminal` not `shell`, `perplexity_search` for web search); 'take the docs as intent and the payload as fact'.

Default is `moonshotai/kimi-k3` via Vercel AI Gateway; the auto-mode safety reviewer is a smaller model (kimi-k3 on Gateway, gpt-5.4-mini on Codex), same classifier shape and same caveat as Claude Code auto mode.

Verdict: not production ready and Vercel does not claim otherwise; the case for it is CI images, JSON mode without TUI scraping, ACP hosting, and a readable system prompt when you spawn an agent per task.

Positioning: 'tiny' = 6.39 MiB download + 10 us cold start + single-digit-MB memory baseline; 'open' = full Zig source under Apache-2.0 (not source-available); 'native' = machine-code binary with no JS runtime plus first-class WebAssembly targets.

Four surfaces, one core: CLI, one-shot `fx ask --json` for scripts/CI, `fx acp` ACP server over stdio, and libfx WebAssembly SDK with `createFxAgent()` (headless) and `createFxTerminal()` (interactive), demonstrated live at fx.sh/try.
The Wasm/embed surface is the one competitors mostly lack: pi has print/JSON/RPC/TS SDK but needs a JS runtime and cannot run in a browser; an HN commenter noted you cannot embed pi in a webpage.

Launch friction was concentrated in providers: default credential order is Vercel OIDC token -> AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY -> `fx login` OAuth -> saved API key, i.e. the default path bills through Vercel AI Gateway (which records model, token counts, latency, cost but does not retain prompts after a request completes).

Version 0.0.5 added Codex and Grok subscription logins, stored locally at ~/.fx/chatgpt-auth.json and ~/.fx/grok-auth.json and never sent to the gateway; a plain documented remote OpenAI-compatible base URL was still missing at publication.
Timeline at publication (Aug 23, 2026): repo created Aug 11, tags from Aug 17-18, HN thread 313 points, ~2,225 stars / 234 forks / 639 commits, v0.0.5.
The sharpest framing in the space: pi (earendil-works/pi, MIT, TypeScript) minimizes *features* while fx minimizes *footprint* - 'one refuses to decide for you, the other refuses to slow you down'.

pi refuses MCP, subagents, permission popups, plan mode, built-in todos and background bash by design (four default tools: read/write/edit/bash); fx embraces all of them (26 documented built-ins, MCP, skills, session-backed subagents, background commands) but compresses the runtime.

Harness spectrum from finished product to raw component: Claude Code (full platform) > pi (composition kit) > fx (micro-native embeddable, below pi despite more features because fx is built to be embedded in larger systems) > tmux + scripts (no harness).
The arithmetic argument for small harnesses: an HN commenter running hierarchical review fleets of 50-100 agents says 6 MB vs 250 MB is 'can do' vs 'cannot'.
Strongest critique: fx ships 26 tools with a tool for nearly every file operation - 'You should have significantly less tools today with how good LLMs have become... Just use Pi.'

Context discipline detail: `memory` persists to ~/.fx/memories.json but is never injected into every request (retrieved on demand); `semantic_search` is explicitly lexical, not an embedding index; large tool results are held out behind byte-range handles read via `read_tool_result`; there are no interactive browser/CDP tools (stated non-goal).

Minimalism ledger: download 6.39 MiB on the homepage vs 7.8 MiB in the README (gap unexplained), 26 built-in tools across nine areas, ~693k lines of Zig across 560 files in src/ - fx is small in runtime surface, not in codebase size.

Unpacked every v0.0.5 release asset: macOS arm64 6.43 MB, Linux arm64 10.13 MB, Linux x86-64 11.87 MB, macOS x86-64 12.31 MB - so the 6.3 MB headline is a representative Apple Silicon build, not a universal artifact size.

The deployment argument rather than the disk argument: one executable removes node_modules, virtualenv, language package manager and separately provisioned runtime from CI images, disposable VMs and evaluation containers, and upgrades/rollbacks become one file plus a checksum.

The startup number's real boundary: with FX_BENCH=1 fx parses arguments, dispatches the CLI path and exits before TTY initialization; Linux CI runs six paths 100x each (fx, help, status --json, background --json, doctor --json, sessions --json) against a 2 ms mean wall-clock budget and fails the PR if exceeded - 'latency is a merge gate'.

Architecture: the same agent loop (model <-> tools <-> policy <-> session) behind three native entry points; `fx acp` lets an editor or host own the interface while fx owns sessions, prompts, tool calls and permission requests.

Small does not mean featureless: file listing/search/read/edit/move/delete, shell commands with background processes, web search and fetch, images, memory, skills, MCP, subagents, scoped AGENTS.md resolution, compaction, persistent sessions, deterministic replay.

Assessment: evaluate fx today as an open implementation of a disposable, embeddable agent runner, not as a stable replacement for an established coding assistant; provider auth, permission behavior and command execution changed substantially within days of release.
Verified setup path: `curl -fsSL https://fx.sh/setup.sh | bash` installs to ~/.local/bin; building from source needs Zig 0.16.0+ (`zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseSafe`).

Three auth routes exactly as documented: `fx login` (Vercel AI Gateway) or `fx setup` (Gateway API key); `fx login codex` (ChatGPT subscription via Codex OAuth); `fx login grok` (X Premium / SuperGrok via xAI OAuth), with subscription tokens stored privately and never sent through the gateway.

Practical details worth copying: sessions auto-name the terminal tab (session name, workspace fallback, model as context) making multi-window work legible; `fx sessions` / `fx session resume last` / `fx session resume --id <id>` form a proper command group; `/fast` on supported Codex models consumes ChatGPT credits at the higher Fast rate.

Security-boundary analysis rather than a review: permissions and sandboxing must not be conflated. At the verified revision the source says an absent sandbox setting means no sandbox, and permission-mode changes do not select one; macOS has an optional OS sandbox, and the source says no OS sandbox implementation was available on unsupported hosts including Linux in that release.

The CLI can execute commands and access files with the authority available to the process, subject to permission checks - so secrets protection and what models/MCP servers/executed code can receive are the user's problem.

WebAssembly surface omits native processes, OS sandboxing, native MCP, subagents, skills, auto-upgrades, arbitrary WASI filesystem access and web search; the browser build requires JavaScript Promise Integration (Chrome/Edge 137+).

Node addon (`libfx`) profile: the headless core advertises no native tools and cannot launch commands or read workspace files unless the host supplies a capability, but a `.node` addon is executable native code with the host process's authority - N-API is not a sandbox.

Skeptical framing worth keeping: the launch materials do not establish that fx completes coding tasks faster, cheaper, more accurately or more safely than competing agents, and no public fx-specific comparative benchmark was found at verification time.

stats.fact: Repository created 2026-08-11; first public tags 2026-08-17/18; first HN launch thread 2026-08-18 reached 318 points
3,237 stars, 364 forks, 250 open issues, Zig (29.8M bytes of code), Apache-2.0, last push 2026-10-01T04:31Z
Latest release v0.0.12 tagged 2026-09-30; release cadence v0.0.5 (Aug 21) -> v0.0.12 (Sep 30) = 8 releases in ~6 weeks

v0.0.12 headline improvements: `fx sessions` on a 14,600-session store dropped from 95 s to 0.17 s (560x) and `fx --resume last` from 33 s to 0.5 s; prompt-too-long now triggers compaction plus one retry; libfx error codes for unsupported model settings renamed (breaking change)

Binary size is target-dependent: macOS arm64 6.43 MB / 6.19 MiB, Linux arm64 10.13 MB, Linux x86-64 11.87 MB, macOS x86-64 12.31 MB; README states a 7.8 MiB production ceiling enforced by macOS arm64 release qualification

Measured startup: `fx --help` 2.7 ms, FX_BENCH dispatch path budget 2 ms mean on Linux CI across six command paths, launch-to-first-model-request 31 ms, vs Claude Code `--help` 112 ms (macOS arm64, Aug 30 2026)

Measured request overhead: 25,479 bytes for a two-word prompt in a clean environment = 17 tool definitions (17,376 B / 68.2%) + 5,531 B system prompt + 2,456 B runtime context + 59 B prompt; ~6,400-7,300 estimated tokens vs Claude Code's 29,061 counted tokens

Skill-catalog tax: same request grows 25,479 -> 42,727 bytes in a populated HOME (16,247 of the extra bytes are one system message listing other agents' skills, e.g. ~/.claude/skills); catalog capped at 16 KiB via skill_catalog_bytes and can be disabled with `off`
npm package `libfx` created 2026-08-17, latest 0.0.12 (modified 2026-09-30), 84 published versions, 'Embed fx agents and terminals in JavaScript hosts'
26 contributors; top contributor fazxes with 2,449 commits out of the project's ~1,082 merged PRs; second is DarlingtonDeveloper (82)

Documented built-in tools number ~26 across nine areas including glob_files, grep_files, read_file, write_file, edit_file, shell (with background run/interact/stop), web_search, web_fetch, vision, skill/install_skill, subagent, capability_search, mcp_select_tool, mcp_features, ask_user_question, read_tool_result

Permission modes are ask / auto (default) / full-access; auto mode runs routine work directly and sends unresolved sensitive actions to a narrow safety reviewer model; piped or redirected stdin stays noninteractive and fails rather than waiting for approval

Model providers: Vercel AI Gateway (default, compiled default model moonshotai/kimi-k3, 233 models in the catalog), Codex via ChatGPT subscription OAuth, Grok via xAI OAuth, plus named custom connections to any OpenAI Chat Completions endpoint (Ollama, vLLM, OpenRouter)
No product telemetry endpoint; auto-update check reads static release metadata every 30 minutes with no machine or installation identifier and can be disabled with FX_AUTO_UPGRADE=0
Embedding surfaces are ACP (`fx acp`), `createFxAgent()` on fx-core.wasm and `createFxTerminal()` on fx-term.wasm; @ai-sdk/harness-fx connects fx to the AI SDK harness layer over ACP
Competitive position checked 2026-10-01: opencode 211,204 stars, claude-code 148,751, pi 110,818, codex (Rust) 127,446 vs fx 3,237 - fx is a fraction of the incumbent harnesses' community size

angles: Cut through the 10-microsecond marketing: explain that the number measures time-before-fx-accepts-input and that the honest figure is a 2 ms CI latency budget plus 2.7 ms to a help screen and 31 ms to a real network request - then show where that actually matters (agent-per-task sandboxes, 50-100 agent fleets) and where it does not (a human typing `fx` once).

The embeddability angle is the real story: four interfaces over one core (shell-like CLI, `fx ask --json` for CI, ACP for editors, WebAssembly libfx for the browser). Explain ACP and libfx with the harness-layer adapter - this is the category Claude Code does not occupy.

Token economics of a harness, not just megabytes: 25.5 KB / ~7K tokens per request vs Claude Code's 29K, of which 68% is tool definitions - and the hidden 68% jump (42.7 KB) from skill-catalog discovery across ~/.claude/skills and friends. A concrete 'what you actually pay per turn' breakdown readers can reproduce with a local mock gateway.

Honest 'who should not use this': no Windows artifacts, no sandbox (permissions are policy, not isolation - especially on Linux), docs that list ~26 tools while the binary sent 17, v0.0.x breaking changes, and local inference documented as an OpenAI-compatible custom connection rather than a one-flag mode.

The 'why another coding agent' fatigue answered with a taxonomy: pi minimizes features, fx minimizes footprint, Claude Code minimizes assembly time - map the harness spectrum from finished platform to raw shell and let readers place themselves.

Billing gravity as a buying consideration: every documented default path flows through Vercel AI Gateway and moonshotai/kimi-k3, with Codex/Grok subscription OAuth and custom connections as the documented exits - including what 'model-agnostic' does and does not mean here.

Practical reviewer framing: a reproducible benchmark recipe (mock gateway via FX_GATEWAY_BASE_URL/FX_GATEWAY_CHAT_URL, empty HOME vs real HOME, byte counting) that separates vendor claims from measured behavior - useful even for readers who never install fx.

notes: Verified primary sources first (GitHub API, fx.sh Markdown docs via llms.txt, HN Algolia item API 49353339, npm registry), then cross-checked five third-party reviews/summaries. All figures carry the date they were checked; several earlier article claims (2,225 stars, v0.0.5/v0.0.7) have been superseded and were updated to 2026-10-01 values. Do not reuse the 7.8 MiB README figure as the measured download size - it is a production ceiling; the Apple Silicon artifact is ~6.2-6.4 MiB. Do not repeat '10 microsecond cold start' without the 2 ms CI budget context.
